Overdraft costs in four charts: daily debt, transaction fees and the next pay deposit

Build a thirty-day ledger that compares two hypothetical fee structures, shows peak borrowing and tests how a starting buffer and pay dates change the cost.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore thirty days of borrowing, transaction fees and daily interest

Interactive planning lab

Flat-fee arrangement · fees plus interest$9.37
Per-debit arrangement · fees plus interest$19.45
Per-debit arrangement · fee-triggering debits3

Hypothetical thirty-day account ledger. Two net pay deposits arrive on the selected first day and fifteen days later; deposits precede all debits on the same day. Separate spending debits occur on the fixed days in the input labels. A zero-dollar debit never triggers a fee. The flat arrangement charges its monthly fee on day 30 even if overdraft was never used. The per-use arrangement charges after every positive debit leaving a negative balance, including a debit that increases an existing overdraft. Fees reduce the account immediately. Daily simple interest is end-of-day debt after transactions and fees times nominal annual rate divided by 365; accrued interest is debited once at the end of day 30. No daily interest-on-interest occurs before that debit. All listed transactions and charges are assumed authorized and funded; the modeled peak debt is not an approved limit. No declined transaction, NSF charge, fee waiver, grace amount, linked-product transfer, actual institution tariff or next-month repayment is calculated.

The central idea

A month can finish with money in the account after borrowing was needed earlier. Count the qualifying debits and negative-balance days, then separate fees, interest and principal owed.

01

A positive monthly total does not fund every earlier bill

The default account starts with CAD 500 and receives two CAD 2,200 net pay deposits, on days five and twenty. Outflows are a CAD 1,800 housing bill on day one, four CAD 400 spending debits on days seven, fourteen, twenty-one and twenty-eight, and a CAD 500 bill on day twelve.

Before borrowing charges, receipts and spending leave CAD 1,000 at month-end: CAD 500 + CAD 4,400 − CAD 3,900. But the first housing bill arrives before either pay deposit. Paying it turns the account balance negative CAD 1,300. The positive final total cannot make that earlier funding requirement disappear.

The model assumes the listed transactions are authorized and funded within an available overdraft arrangement. It does not establish an approved limit or guarantee that a bank will process a payment. The FCAC overdraft guide explains the product’s general mechanics and the need to check the agreement.

02

State exactly which transaction triggers a charge

The first hypothetical arrangement charges a flat CAD 5 on day thirty, even if borrowing was not used. The second charges CAD 5 after every positive debit that leaves the account negative. That includes a debit that increases an overdraft already outstanding. A zero-dollar debit is ignored.

In the default per-debit case, the housing payment triggers the first fee. After the first salary arrives and the next spending debit is paid, the day-twelve bill takes the account below zero again and triggers another fee. The day-fourteen debit increases that negative balance and triggers a third fee.

This is a defined teaching structure, not a universal meaning of “pay per use.” Agreements may charge differently, waive fees, use thresholds or group transactions by day. Counting only transitions from positive to negative would undercount this example’s fees because it would overlook the debit that adds to an existing overdraft.

03

Calculate the interest on the balance that is actually negative

Both examples assume a 21% nominal annual borrowing rate. At the end of each day, after deposits, spending and applicable fees, interest accrues as the negative balance multiplied by 21% divided by 365. A positive or zero balance incurs no overdraft interest.

The daily interest accrues separately until it is debited after day thirty. The model does not charge daily interest on previously accrued but unposted interest during this month. Fees, however, reduce cash immediately when they are charged, so they can increase the interest-bearing balance.

Under the defaults, the flat arrangement incurs approximately CAD 4.37 of interest and CAD 5 of fees. The per-debit arrangement incurs approximately CAD 4.45 of interest and CAD 15 of fees. Total charges are therefore about CAD 9.37 and CAD 19.45. These are independently calculated illustrations; they are not current institution quotations or an estimate of the account’s annual borrowing cost.

04

Keep the cash bridge separate from the price of borrowing

The peak-borrowing bars answer how far below zero the account goes. In the default, the largest negative balance is CAD 1,300 under the flat arrangement and CAD 1,305 under per-debit fees. That amount measures a cash bridge, while the fee-and-interest bars measure its modeled cost.

A deposit first reduces the negative account balance before leaving positive cash. The model does not treat the overdraft as free savings, count its limit as income or assume that interest payments reduce the principal. A plan can have a modest charge and still need a substantial amount of money before payday.

The default flat arrangement has ten days with a negative end-of-day transaction balance before the final interest debit. The per-debit arrangement has twelve. Fees can make a nearly balanced day negative and keep it negative until another receipt. The two paths therefore need separate ledgers rather than a common debt balance with two fee totals attached afterward.

05

Test the buffer and the pay date without changing monthly pay

The matrix replaces opening cash and the first pay date. The second pay deposit always follows fifteen days later. All pay amounts and spending dates remain selected, so the comparison changes timing and the initial buffer rather than quietly increasing earnings.

Each cell reports the per-debit arrangement’s fees plus interest for this one modeled month. It is not the opening cash required to avoid all borrowing and is not a prediction of future bank fees. A smaller charge can coexist with an outstanding overdraft at the end, which must be read from the actual cash path.

Deposits precede debits when they share a day in this example. Real processing order, holds and cut-off times may differ. If a payment and salary are close together, verify when money becomes available instead of assuming their shared calendar date guarantees sufficient funds.

06

Use actual transaction history before changing the arrangement

  1. List deposits and required payments by their actual availability dates.
  2. Separate fee-triggering transactions from days with debt outstanding.
  3. Check the agreement’s fee definitions, waivers, limits and repayment conditions.
  4. Reconstruct daily balances and interest using the institution’s convention.
  5. Test a realistic opening buffer or an agreed change to a bill date.
  6. Review whether the shortfall repeats in later months.

The model excludes declined payments, NSF charges, linked-account transfers and subsequent-month repayment. It does not compare an authorized overdraft with an unauthorized missed payment or assess eligibility for credit. Its purpose is to show why monthly averages, transaction counts and borrowing days belong together. Reducing charges can help, but a recurring gap also needs a household cash-flow plan and a feasible reserve-building schedule.
